newsitem.title: POLAND: FEATURE - Poland needs austerity or flood sinks its success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Poland needs austerity or flood sinks its success.

text.p: Whoever forms Poland's next government after September elections will be forced to impose unpopular fiscal tightening or face a serious economic crisis in 1998.

Analysts say that without renewed financial austerity the economy, already overheating with trade and current account deficits dangerously booming because of high domestic demand, may not withstand the additional negative impact of recent floods.

The chief contestants of the election, the ruling ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and rightist Solidarity Election Action (AWS), both pledge responsible financial policies if they win but remain silent on the necessary tightening that would have to include spending cuts.

"It is natural that before the elections politicians are silent on the issue, public spending cuts are unpopular," said Bohdan Wyznikiewicz, an analyst at the Market Economy Research Institute (IBnGR).

The reformed ex-communists, in power since 1993 through an alliance with the populist peasant party (PSL) have so far ignored calls from the central bank and international insitutions urging a balanced budget in 1997. Yet the zloty's dive by five percent in one day in May could be a taste of things to come if they keep dodging the issue.

As for now they plan to cut the budget gap to 1.9 percent of GDP in 1998 from 2.8 percent planned for this year. But the impact of the flooding will come into the equation too, possibly boosting the deficit well above three percent this year.
The Solidarity union, whose many members helped overthrow communism in 1989 but lost power four years later because of infighting, also promises a tight 1998 budget.
"Limiting it (the budget deficit) is needed because otherwise we will see inflation increasing," Janusz Tomaszewski, AWS deputy head, told Reuters.
SOLIDARITY REASSURES FOREIGN INVESTORS
Tomaszewski, whose group encompasses more than small 30 rightist parties led by Solidarity, says his party's union roots would not prevent it from pursuing sound economic policies.
"Foreign investors can sleep at ease...If the AWS has an influence forming the government it will not allow the current account deficit and other pending issues to become a serious problem," he said.

He said the AWS's recent proposal to issue special bonds to finance the flood relief programme rather than borrow from the central bank and abroad as the government wants, showed his group had better economic ideas.
Foreign market analysts said they were not afraid of either the continued ex-communists' rule or an AWS takeover but their support leaned towards the SLD because it was a party they already knew.
HUNG PARLIAMENT FEARS
They said they feared the elections would result in a fractured parliament, in which no clear majority emerged.
"All we would like to see is a solid, clear result and not a weak unstable coalition of four of five parties," said Robert Beange, economist at Lehman Brothers in London.
Most fears concerned the Polish Peasant Party (PSL), now the smaller partner in the ruling coalition, and the right-radical Movement for the Independent Poland (ROP).
The PSL opposes cutting the budget deficit and is seen as an enemy of quick privatisation, notably that involving foreign capital, while the ROP advocates protectionist trade measures.
"The financial markets would be concerned if the PSL or ROP gained much ground in the elections," ABN-AMRO bank said in a report on Poland.
The perception of the new government also depends on what happens to the liberal Union for Freedom (UW), grouping intellectuals and market reformers who launched reforms in the early 1990s.
Any government including the UW would be likely to be welcomed by investors even though they would prefer the party to link up with the former communists.
Such an alliance would be anathema for a huge number of UW activists and an opinion poll on Tuesday showed many voters would like it to team up with the AWS.
Support for such an alliance was expressed by 20 percent of people polled by the PBS polling organisation compared with 12.4 percent for the existing coalition.

"The floods in southern Poland had a decisive influence on the change in voter preferences and offset the earlier negative perceptions of the AWS from infighting within that group," said PBS analyst Ryszard Gudyka.

Some analysts said that while both the ex-communists and Solidarity were likely to pursue tight financial policies the union-linked AWS may be less willing to tackle the much-needed reform of heavy loss-making industries.

"In terms of macroeconomic policy I am not overly concerned with the AWS but I'm just worried that when it comes to structural reform they will not have the metal, whereas the SLD seem to have it," said Joseph Karazin, chief economist at Societe Generale in London.
